<reason>B (PRO) won. Both opened strongly and stayed well-grounded with no fake sourcing. The debate's pivot was engineered by B: Pressure Q2 forced A to state whether any fine design was acceptable, and in Rebuttal 2 A conceded "a genuine last-resort penalty for documented bad-faith refusal" — the motion's operative core. B's closing converted that concession decisively. B also neutralized A's main "you rewrote the motion" attack with a genuinely clever semantic argument: "repeatedly" logically entails documented prior failures (i.e., notice and process), and "meaningful" entails proportionality, so the safeguards A claimed were invented were read into the text by fair interpretation. Meanwhile, A never named any tool in its toolkit that reaches the well-resourced willful refuser — B's central, unanswered question from Rebuttal 1 onward. A's capacity critique (vendor-locked systems, fines extracting compliance budgets) was real and remained partially live, since B's "engagement means you never reach a third failure" assumed exactly what A disputed. But A's own concession deflated the blunt-instrument framing, and B's self-selection weighing made the remaining dispute easier to resolve in B's favor. Clear but competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive sequence was B's Pressure Q2 ("is there any fine design you would accept?") → A's Rebuttal 2 concession accepting a last-resort fine for documented bad-faith repeat refusal → B's closing pounce ("That is the motion"). Within a single speech, B's Rebuttal 2 A1 ("repetition is the warning system; meaningful is relational") was the sharpest standalone move, collapsing A's textualist attack while the self-selection argument absorbed A's sympathetic small-clinic defendant.</best_rebuttal>
